versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Then Joseph could no longer control himself before all his attendants, and he cried out, “Send everyone away from me!”
So none of them were with Joseph when he made himself known to his brothers. 2 But he wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard him, and Pharaoh’s household soon heard of it.
3 Joseph said to his brothers, “I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?”
But they were unable to answer him, because they were terrified in his presence.
4 Then Joseph said to his brothers, “Please come near me.” And they did so.

“I am Joseph, your brother,” he said, “the one you sold into Egypt! 5 And now, do not be distressed or angry with yourselves that you sold me into this place, because it was to save lives that God sent me before you. 6 For the famine has covered the land these two years, and there will be five more years without plowing or harvesting. 7 God sent me before you to preserve you as a remnant on the earth and to save your lives by a great deliverance. 8 Therefore it was not you who sent me here, but God, who has made me a father to Pharaoh—lord of all his household and ruler over all the land of Egypt.

context_lines: After Judah's appeal, Joseph can no longer contain his emotion. He sends the attendants away and reveals himself to his brothers, weeping loudly enough for the Egyptians to hear. The ruler before whom they have been pleading identifies himself as the brother they sold.

The brothers are terrified and cannot answer. Joseph calls them closer and repeats who he is. His next words address their distress: God sent him ahead to save lives. The famine has lasted two years, and five more remain. His position in Egypt will preserve the family through the danger still ahead.

Joseph speaks of the same events from two perspectives. His brothers sold him, and he names that action directly. God has brought him to a place where their lives can be preserved. The saving purpose does not make the betrayal disappear; it explains why he can now meet them with reassurance instead of revenge.

He describes his position as a father to Pharaoh, lord of the royal household, and ruler over Egypt. These words convey the influence and responsibility that make his offer of help possible. The family has finally learned what the reader has watched developing through slavery, prison, and appointment.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read Joseph's explanation as God's ability to bring saving good from human wrongdoing, alongside Joseph's willingness to forgive. [Wesley's notes on Genesis 45:5–8](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) distinguish the good God brings from the brothers' sinful intent. The [Catholic Catechism, paragraph 312](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_one/section_two/chapter_one/article_1/paragraph_4_the_creator.html), likewise uses Joseph's story to explain that good brought from evil does not make the evil itself good.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: [Acts 7:9–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/7.htm) directly recalls Joseph's rejection, God's presence with him, and his making himself known on the second visit. The rejected brother has become the means of preserving the family. Joseph's explanation here lets them see how the earlier suffering fits into that rescue.

His tears and invitation to draw near also offer a comparison with God's compassion toward returning sinners. [Wesley's notes on Genesis 45:1–3](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) connect the scene with the father's welcome in [Luke 15:20–24](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/15.htm). The comparison concerns mercy that welcomes people whose wrongdoing is real. Reconciliation becomes possible without pretending that nothing happened.
